query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single-step post‐fabrication compression plasma flow (CPF) treatment of tungsten particles pre‐coated with a thin, vapor‐deposited copper layer will yield a fine, intermixing W(Cu) solid solution that minimizes voids and phase separation, thereby achieving improved thermal transport and radiation resistance while maintaining mechanical durability via rapid localized melting and ensuing non-equilibrium solidification at the tungsten/copper interface.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite consisting of discrete or connected tungsten particles or regions embedded in a copper matrix (or with the tungsten surfaces initially coated with copper via vapor deposition) with conventional processing defects such as interfacial voids and phase separation.
generation.intervention: Apply a brief, high-energy compression plasma flow (CPF) treatment with parameters that induce localized melting of the copper coating and the tungsten surface, followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: The CPF treatment should be carried out with brief pulses and a moderate energy density under a controlled atmosphere (for example, using a plasma-forming gas like nitrogen) to limit unwanted nitride formation, and within temperature levels that do not overheat the bulk to compromise mechanical integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a homogenized, metastable W(Cu) solid solution at the particle–matrix interface, characterized by a fine crystallite structure with numerous intergranular boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The CPF treatment induces rapid local melting and mixing at the tungsten/copper interface; the rapid cooling leads to non‐equilibrium solidification, suppressing void formation and phase separation, thus enhancing the interfacial contact and thermal connectivity while preserving load‐bearing microstructural features.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional methods (e.g., mechanical alloying or conventional sintering), the CPF‐treated composite is expected to show reduced interfacial voids and phase inhomogeneities, leading to superior thermal conductivity and enhanced radiation resistance along with maintained or improved mechanical durability under fusion‐reactor joint conditions.
generation.baseline: Traditional processing routes such as filling tungsten skeletons with molten copper, spark plasma sintering, or powder mixing methods, which typically yield voids and phase separations that impair thermal transport and mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold for composite structures operating within the thermal load and irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints (operational temperatures up to ~1500–2000 K and modest irradiation doses); however, long-term mechanical degradation due to differential thermal expansion or residual stresses under extreme service cycles remains to be fully assessed.
generation.uncertainty: Although preliminary evidence suggests that CPF can induce a beneficial interfacial alloying and rapid solidification effect, the scaling uniformity over large-area joints, potential residual stress distributions, and long-term performance under repeated irradiation and thermal cycling are still uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-copper composites with identical initial microstructures. Subject one set to the proposed CPF treatment with a thin vapor-deposited copper coating, while keeping the other as a control processed by the standard method. Use identical thermal and irradiation exposure in a simulated fusion reactor joint environment. Characterize the microstructure, void content, thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability (e.g., tensile strength, fracture toughness) before and after simulated irradiation.
measurements: High-resolution electron microscopy to quantify void size and distribution at the W-Cu interface
X-ray diffraction and peak shift analysis to confirm formation of the W(Cu) solid solution
Thermal diffusivity measurements (e.g., via laser flash analysis)
Mechanical testing (tensile, fracture toughness) both pre- and post-irradiation
Irradiation-induced defect quantification via ion implantation surrogate experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CPF-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in voids and phase separation, nor show improved thermal transport and mechanical durability (compared to the untreated controls) under simulated fusion-relevant irradiation and thermal cycling, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, creating alloys based on tungsten and copper using compression plasma flows is proposed. This type of surface treatment is pulsed and allows transferring a sufficiently high energy density to the surface layer, which is necessary for its melting [,,,]. A feature of this type of treatment is the high cooling rates of the formed melt, which ensure that the processes related to the formation of the structure and phases during crystallization are non-equilibrium. Due to the high cooling rates, it is possible to achieve the condition of partial mixing of tungsten and copper in the liquid state, forming an alloy of a composite structure. In this work, it is proposed to use the effect of compression plasma flows in order to modify the structural state of the near-surface tungsten layer. Furthermore, in the case of the preliminary application of a copper coating to the surface of tungsten samples, exposure to compression plasma flows makes it possible to create an alloy based on tungsten and copper by means of their liquid-phase mixing.

Overall, the work demonstrated the fundamental opportunity of creating alloys based on tungsten and copper by successively applying copper coating to the tungsten surface and using pulsed action of compression plasma flows with a pulse duration of 100 μs, with an absorbed energy density of 35–55 J/cm2. The results demonstrate the formation of a composite structure based on individual phases of tungsten and copper, and due to the high-speed crystallization of the molten surface layer, a solid solution of W(Cu) with a distorted crystal lattice is formed. Analysis of radiation effects during irradiation of tungsten and tungsten-copper alloy samples with helium ions with an energy of 40 keV and doses of (1–3) × 1017 cm−2 showed that tungsten samples pre-treated with CPF in the melting and mixing mode of the near-surface layer have increased radiation resistance. In the near-surface region, corresponding to the helium ion range, there is a distortion of the tungsten phase crystal lattice, which causes mechanical destruction of the surface.
